rationale: Evidence from iteration 5 (score 484.6, best so far): the oval finishes 20/20 (2.00 s, 0.5 line-loss events per run). The s-bend improved to 4/20 finishes and 0.77 progress, up from 0.47. The slalom is unchanged at about 0.17 progress, 0/20 finishes, and 1.0 line-loss event per run, and every slalom run ends off_track. Iteration 5 changed three things at once (sensors forward to y=0.06, kp 6.5/kd 2.0, base_speed 1.0 with track 0.10). The slalom did not respond to any of them, which suggests the slalom failure is not about bend-entry timing or turning agility. The consistent single line loss followed by off-track points to the array losing the tape when the robot is offset on a sharp swing. The current array spans only +/-0.06 m, and the 16 mm footprints cannot see the 25 mm tape once the robot is about 0.04 m off centre on the outer sensors. The change is to widen the array to +/-0.08 m (the allowed maximum) with 7 sensors at 0.027 m spacing, so the tape stays under at least one sensor for larger lateral errors. Weights run linearly from -1 to +1, so the steering signal keeps the same scale and kp/kd stay unchanged, which isolates the sensing change. The off-track limit is still max(0.06, 0.0125+0.03)=0.06 m for this body, so the body is kept at 0.12 m. Expected result: fewer or no line-loss events on the slalom and s-bend, and slalom progress rising well above 0.17. The oval should still finish near 2.0 s. Risks: a wider array may slightly blunt the response on straights, and extra sensors add reading noise to the average. Hypotheses: H1, the line is lost because the outer sensors leave the tape on slalom swings (tested by widening). H2, the lost tape is not caused by lag, so the forward move from y=0.04 to y=0.06 was neutral. Measurements wanted next: line_loss_events and max_error per track to see whether the first loss still happens and how far off centre the robot gets, progress and completion per track for the slalom and s-bend, and steering_oscillation to check for chatter from the extra sensors.
